judge_assessment.explanation: I re-derived every classification from the TikZ coordinates in worksheet.tex rather than from the rendered picture, and the judge is right on all of it. Problem 1: A (0,0)-(1.7,0)-(1.7,1.7)-(0,1.7) and B (0,0)-(2.4,0)-(2.4,1.2)-(0,1.2) have four right angles, C and D do not — 2. Problem 3, 'exactly one pair of parallel sides': A's opposite side vectors are (2.2,0)/(2.2,0) and (0.6,1.4)/(0.6,1.4), so A is a parallelogram with two pairs and is correctly excluded; B and C each have one pair; D is a square — 2. Problem 8: A, B and D are parallelograms and C is the trapezoid Kim must take back out — 3, with the declared trap 3+1 = 4 exactly matching a child who counts the trapezoid. Problems 7 and 9 include the rotated square (1.2,0)-(2.4,1.2)-(1.2,2.4)-(0,1.2), whose sides are all 1.697 cm and whose angles are all right, so it belongs in both the equal-sides group and the square-corners group — 3 and 2. Problem 6's line plot draws 0:3, 1:2, 2:2, 3:0, 4:5, giving 12 cards with mode 4, and the impossibility claim in 6(c) is sound (three right angles force the fourth). Three items are correctly typed manual, matching the judge's manual_items_reviewed: 3. Where I part company is on coverage. Problem 8 prints THREE responses — circle the cards, write how many there are, and 'write the letter of the card Kim should take back out' — and verify.json id 8 has one entry, expected 3; the letter C is a determinate answer nothing records. More broadly, six problems (1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9) require the child to CIRCLE cards, and only the resulting count is verified, so a child who circles the wrong two cards and writes '2' is machine-indistinguishable from one who circles the right two. The answer key names the cards ('Circle A and B'), so the grader is served; verify.json is not, and neither is the manual declaration.

strengths_to_preserve: The attribute groups deliberately do not nest, and the key says so: after problem 2 it prints 'Notice that this group is not the same group as problem 1: card A is in this group and not in that one, and card B is in that group and not this one.' That is the actual content of 3.G.A and most worksheets on this topic never make it visible.

Problems 7 and 9 include a square drawn at 45 degrees (the diamond at (1.2,0)-(2.4,1.2)-(1.2,2.4)-(0,1.2)), which defeats the standard misconception that a square is the one sitting flat. I confirmed its four sides are equal and its four angles right, so it correctly belongs in both the equal-sides and square-corners groups.

Item 6(c) — why a four-sided shape can never have exactly three square corners — is declared manual rather than reduced to a number, and it is the one item on the sheet that requires an argument rather than a count. The line plot's deliberate gap above 3 is what makes the question askable.

Problem 8's trap is declared as expr '3 + 1', value 4, which is precisely Kim's error (counting the trapezoid), so the planted wrong result is machine-proved distinguishable and prints under 'Common wrong answers'.

All three manual items (5, 6c, 10) carry acceptance criteria in their desc rather than a single model answer, and item 10's drawing task correctly takes no answer line — the drawing is the answer, on genuine dot paper.

root_causes.description: A multi-part item can print a third response with a determinate answer while its id carries a single entry, because no gate compares printed answer slots against covered verify entries.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 8: 'Circle the cards that really belong, write how many there are, and write the letter of the card Kim should take back out.'
verify.json id 8: one entry, {"type": "read_data", "query": "total", "expected": 3} with the 3+1 trap. The letter C appears nowhere in the verification data.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '8. 3' — one value for an item asking for three things.
By contrast, problems 4 and 6 DO carry two and three entries respectively for their lettered parts, so the sheet knows how to do this and problem 8 simply did not.

root_causes.description: Six of the ten problems ask the student to circle cards — a marked response that IS the classification work — and record only the resulting count as machine-verified, with no manual companion declaring the marks for human review. The count is a lossy proxy: it cannot distinguish a correct sort from a wrong sort of the same size, which on a four-card item is a one-in-three chance of passing by accident.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problems 1, 2, 3, 7, 9 all read 'Circle every card ... then write how many cards you circled'; problem 8 reads 'Circle the cards that really belong'.

verify.json ids 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9 are all single read_data 'total' entries (2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2). Each entry's data dict does name the per-card membership ({"card A": 1, "card B": 1, "card C": 0, "card D": 0}), but only the total is the expected answer, so the per-card assignment is never a checked or declared response.
On problems 1, 2, 3 and 9 the expected count is 2 out of 4 cards, so there are six ways to circle two cards and only one is right — five wrong sorts produce the correct printed number.
The answer key does name them ('Circle A and B', 'Circle A and C'), which is why this is a contract gap rather than a grading failure.

improvements.title: Count printed answer slots per problem and require one covered verify entry for each
improvements.proposed_change: Extend tests/check_answer_line.py (already takes the worksheet .tex plus verify.json, already build.sh gate 10) to count answer-location macros per segmented problem region and compare with the number of verify entries for that id carrying an 'expected' value or "type": "manual", failing on an undercount. For curr-098 the fix is one JSON entry: id 8 gains a check for the letter Kim must remove — a read_data entry over the same {"card A": 1, "card B": 1, "card C": 0, "card D": 1} dict with a query that names the excluded card, or, if no query fits, an explicit entry recording 'C'. Problems 4 and 6 on this same sheet already demonstrate the multi-entry-per-id pattern, so no new convention is needed.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/fixtures/slot_undercount_quads/ with a worksheet problem reading 'Circle the cards that really belong,~\ansblank and write the letter of the card Kim should take back out.~\ansblank' against a verify.json id-1 holding one read_data total entry (expected 3). Assert check_answer_line.py exits 1 with '2 printed answer slots, 1 covered'; add the second entry and assert exit 0.
improvements.expected_impact: Closes the run's largest verification gap. On this sheet the effect is small and precise — one unchecked letter becomes checked — which is exactly the kind of quiet omission a per-problem contract misses and a per-slot contract catches.
improvements.risk: Low here. The general risk is authors deleting scaffold blanks rather than declaring them; the failure message must lead with 'declare the value'.

improvements.title: Circling and sorting items need a manual entry recording WHICH cards belong, not only how many
improvements.proposed_change: Add the open-response stem scan to tests/check_answer_line.py covering marking verbs ('circle', 'cross', 'mark', 'shade', 'draw', 'sketch') alongside explanation verbs, exiting 1 when the matching id has no {"type": "manual"} entry. For curr-098, ids 1, 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9 each keep their count check and gain a manual entry naming the members — 'the circled cards must be exactly A and B' — which the answer key already states verbatim for every one of them, so the entries can be lifted from existing prose. Better still, and worth considering as a follow-up: since each entry's data dict already encodes membership per card, a 'membership' query type would let the sort be machine-checked rather than merely declared, at which point the manual entry becomes unnecessary. Record that as the preferred long-term shape in references/problem-library.md's reframing section, which already teaches how to turn understanding tasks into checkable ones.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/fixtures/circling_unflagged/ with a worksheet problem reading 'Circle every card below that has four square corners. Then write how many cards you circled.~\ansblank' against a verify.json id-1 holding only {"type": "read_data", "query": "total", "data": {"card A": 1, "card B": 1, "card C": 0, "card D": 0}, "expected": 2}. Assert check_answer_line.py exits 1 naming problem 1 and the verb 'Circle'; append {"id": 1, "type": "manual", "desc": "the circled cards must be exactly A and B"} and assert exit 0.
improvements.expected_impact: A sorting sheet stops reporting itself as fully machine-verified when what it verifies is a count that five wrong sorts also produce. The grader gains an explicit membership statement in the verification record rather than having to reconstruct it from the key's prose.
improvements.risk: 'circle' is a shape noun in geometry, so the scan must run on stem text only and tolerate 'draw a circle' style false positives with a cheap one-line fix. Flagging six of ten problems manual on one sheet will also make the build exit 2 loudly; the membership-query follow-up is the better end state and should not be delayed too long behind the manual declaration.

case_summary: Mathematically the most rigorous sheet in this batch. I re-derived every quadrilateral from its TikZ coordinates rather than trusting the render, and every classification is correct — including the rotated square in problems 7 and 9 (four 1.697 cm sides, four right angles, so it belongs in both groups), the parallelogram correctly excluded from 'exactly one pair of parallel sides' in problem 3, and Kim's trapezoid in problem 8. The line plot totals 12 with mode 4, and the impossibility argument in 6(c) is sound. Three items are properly declared manual with real acceptance criteria, and the key's observation that the problem-1 and problem-2 groups do not nest is the actual content of the standard. Two contract gaps remain. Problem 8 asks for three things and verifies one: the letter of the card Kim must remove is a determinate answer nothing records. And six problems are built on circling cards while only the resulting count is checked — on a four-card item with an expected count of two, five wrong sorts produce the right number — with no manual entry declaring the marks for review. The membership is already in each entry's data dict and already spelled out in the answer key, so both fixes are additive. Worth recording as checked and cleared: problem 2's card A is drawn (0,0)-(1.7,0)-(2.3,1.6)-(0.6,1.6), whose slanted sides measure 1.709 cm against 1.700 cm horizontals — 0.09 mm from a true rhombus on a sheet that invites measurement, which is below any ruler's resolution and not a defect, though the exact coordinate would be 1.5906 rather than 1.6.
